extract:
Chet Baker was born Chesney Henry Baker Jr. in Yale, Oklahoma, in 1929, and moved with his family to Southern California as a boy. He became one of the defining figures of West Coast cool jazz in the early 1950s, and he stayed active, through long stretches of turmoil, until his death in Amsterdam in 1988. He learned trumpet in school and played in Army bands while stationed in Berlin and later San Francisco. Back in Los Angeles he worked jam sessions around the city's clubs. In 1952 he played with Charlie Parker on the leader's West Coast engagements, a credential that quickly raised his profile.

His breakthrough came that same year in Gerry Mulligan's pianoless quartet, which recorded for Richard Bock's Pacific Jazz label. The group's version of "My Funny Valentine" made Chet Baker a star almost overnight. His lyrical, vibrato-light trumpet tone, shaped by the restraint of Miles Davis and Bix Beiderbecke, became a model of the cool sound. After Mulligan's arrest broke up the quartet, Chet Baker led his own groups, most notably with pianist Russ Freeman. He continued with Pacific Jazz, cutting Chet Baker & Strings, the Chet Baker Ensemble sessions, and the live Jazz At Ann Arbor. His fragile, unadorned singing became equally central to his appeal. Chet Baker Sings, featuring "But Not for Me," "Time After Time," and "I Fall in Love Too Easily," split critics but found a devoted audience and grew into his signature album.

In 1955 and 1956 he toured Europe, and in Paris he recorded the Barclay sessions later issued as the Chet Baker in Paris volumes. These included quintet dates with Belgian saxophonist and flutist Bobby Jaspar. Pianist Dick Twardzik, a member of his touring band, died of an overdose in Paris during that trip, an early shadow of the heroin addiction that would dominate Chet Baker's life. Back in the United States he recorded for Riverside, and he contributed to Theme Music From "The James Dean Story," a fitting pairing given the matinee-idol image that photographer William Claxton had helped create. Drug arrests followed in the United States and Europe, including a jail term in Italy. After his release came Chet Is Back!, recorded in Rome with European players. Mid-1960s sessions such as The Most Important Jazz Album Of 1964/65 found him switching to flugelhorn and working in a harder-edged setting.

A 1968 beating that damaged his teeth and embouchure nearly ended his career. He rebuilt his playing in the 1970s, recording with producer Creed Taylor's CTI label on She Was Too Good to Me. He then spent most of his final decade in Europe, recording prolifically for small labels, often in drummerless trios. Bruce Weber's documentary Let's Get Lost (1988) captured his ravaged late-life persona and charisma.

Chet Baker died on May 13, 1988, after falling from a hotel window in Amsterdam. His recordings, especially the Pacific Jazz vocal sides, remain touchstones of cool jazz and of intimate jazz singing, influencing vocalists and trumpeters alike. Biographies, Weber's film, and the 2015 Ethan Hawke biopic Born to Be Blue have kept his story in wide circulation.
title: Chet Baker
